_comment: THE ONE PLACE THAT KNOWS WHAT 'FAST ENOUGH' MEANS.
Read by all three consumers so a number can never drift between them:
- src/test/perf/scorecard.ts   (scoring, and the vitest that proves the scoring)
- scripts/perf/route-bundles.mjs (the per-route JS budget check in CI)
- e2e/perf/scorecard.spec.ts   (the Playwright + CDP measurement run)
Every threshold is an INCLUSIVE ceiling unless its name says otherwise: a route
passes at exactly the budget and fails above it. `cls` is the one exclusive bound
(Core Web Vitals defines 'good' as < 0.1, not <= 0.1).
Raising a number here is a deliberate act that shows up in a diff and needs a
reason in the PR. That is the point of the file — a budget nobody can quietly
widen inside the check that enforces it.
The two device profiles every route is measured on. The mobile numbers are
Lighthouse's 'Slow 4G' shape, which is what the brief calls Fast 3G/4G: a
throughput and latency pair chosen to be reproducible, not to model one
carrier. CPU slowdown is applied through CDP Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate.
This is a retired-expat product bought on a phone. Mobile is the real profile;
desktop is measured so a regression that only shows on one is still visible.
WHAT A ROUTE IS ALLOWED TO BE TODAY, on the way to what `thresholds` says it
must become. The CI gate enforces THIS; the scorecard reports against
`thresholds`. Both read this one file.
WHY A RATCHET AND NOT THE TARGETS. A gate set to the 10/10 numbers is red on
the day it lands, because the platform is not at 10/10 yet — and a gate that
is red on arrival protects nothing and is deleted within a week. This one is
green now and can only ever be tightened, so it defends every improvement the
moment it lands instead of waiting for the last one.
HOW TO CHANGE IT. Down, by running `npm run perf:budgets:record` after an
improvement and committing the diff. Never up: a number that has to rise is a
regression, and it belongs in the PR description rather than in this file.
A route with no entry is held to `thresholds` — which is the finished state,
so deleting an entry is how a route graduates.
WHAT IS RATCHETED, AND WHAT IS ONLY REPORTED. Only numbers a MACHINE cannot
change: the query count, the N+1 set, the gzipped bytes, and CLS — which is a
property of the layout rather than of the clock.
LCP and long tasks are deliberately absent. The first version of the CI gate
ratcheted them and went red on its own first run: `join.wizard` measured
2,544 ms where the ratchet was recorded and 4,071 ms on the GitHub runner,
which is simply a slower machine, with nothing about the application changed.
A wall-clock ceiling recorded on one machine cannot gate another — widen the
headroom enough to survive the difference and it catches nothing; leave it
narrow and it goes red for whoever the noisy neighbour is. They are printed by
the job instead, and held to account by `npm run perf:measure`, which is run
deliberately on a known machine.
HEADROOM. A query count gets none: the recorded value is already the high water
mark of the runs that produced it (cc.alerts measured 28 on one run and 17 on
the next, as different realtime reads land), and inflating it further would
hide a real extra query. Bytes get 2%, enough for a dependency patch release.
CLS gets 20%, for the part of it that is timing-dependent — whether an image
lands before or after first paint.
Per-route budget exceptions. EVERY entry must carry a `reason`, and the
scorecard prints it beside the route so an exception can never look like a
pass. An override loosens one named threshold for one route; it never
switches a check off.
